{{Short description|Statistical rule for bin-width in histograms}}
In [[statistics]], the '''Freedman&ndash;Diaconis rule''' can be used to select the width of the bins to be used in a [[histogram]].<ref name="fd">{{cite journal|last1=Freedman|first1=David|last2=Diaconis|first2=Persi|date=December 1981|title=On the histogram as a density estimator: ''L''<sub>2</sub> theory|journal=Probability Theory and Related Fields|volume=57|issue=4|pages=453–476|doi=10.1007/BF01025868|issn=0178-8051|author-link=David Freedman (statistician)|author-link2=Persi Diaconis|s2cid=14437088 }}</ref> It is named after [[David A. Freedman]] and [[Persi Diaconis]].

For a set of empirical measurements sampled from some [[probability distribution]], the Freedman–Diaconis rule is designed to approximately minimize the integral of the squared difference between the [[histogram]] (i.e., relative frequency density) and the density of the theoretical probability distribution.

In detail, the Integrated Mean Squared Error (IMSE) is
:<math>
\text{IMSE} = E\left[ \int_I (H(x) - f(x))^2 \right]
</math>
where <math>H</math> is the histogram approximation of <math>f</math> on the interval <math>I</math> computed with <math>n</math> data points sampled from the distribution <math>f</math>. <math>E[\cdot]</math> denotes the [[Expected value|expectation]] across many independent draws of <math>n</math> data points. Under mild conditions, namely that <math>f</math> and its first two derivatives are [[Square-integrable function|
<math>L^2</math>]], Freedman and Diaconis show that the integral is minimised by choosing the bin width

:<math>
h^* = \left( 6 / \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f'(x)^2 dx \right)^{1/3}n^{-1/3}
</math>

A formula which was derived earlier by Scott.<ref>{{cite journal
| doi = 10.1093/biomet/66.3.605
| author = D.W. Scott 
| year = 1979
| title = On optimal and data-based histograms
| journal = Biometrika
| volume = 66
| issue = 3
| pages = 605–610 
| jstor = 2335182
}}
</ref> Swapping the order of the integration and expectation is justified by [[Fubini's Theorem|Fubini's theorem]]. The Freedman–Diaconis rule is derived by assuming that <math>f</math> is a [[Normal distribution]], making it an example of a ''normal reference rule''. In this case
<math>\int f'(x)^2 = (2 \sqrt{2\pi} \sigma^3)^{-1}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Scott | first1 = D.W. | year = 2009 | title = Sturges' rule | journal = WIREs Computational Statistics | volume = 1 | issue = 3| pages = 303–306 | doi=10.1002/wics.35| s2cid = 197483064 }}</ref>

Freedman and Diaconis use the [[interquartile range]] to estimate the [[standard deviation]]: <math>\sigma \sim \Phi^{-1}(0.75) - \Phi^{-1}(0.25)</math><ref name="scott">
{{cite journal
| doi = 10.1002/wics.103
| author = D.W. Scott 
| year = 2010
| title = Scott's Rule
| publisher = Wiley
| journal = Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews: Computational Statistics
| volume = 2
| issue = 4
| pages = 497–502}}
</ref> where <math>\Phi</math> is the [[cumulative distribution function]] for a normal density. This gives the rule

:<math>\text{Bin width}=2\, { \text{IQR}(x) \over{  \sqrt[3]{n}  }}</math>

where <math>\operatorname{IQR}(x) </math> is the [[interquartile range]] of the data and <math> n </math> is the number of observations in the sample <math> x </math>. In fact if the normal density is used the factor  2 in front comes out to be <math>\sim 2.59</math>,<ref name="scott" /> but 2 is the factor recommended by Freedman and Diaconis.

==Other approaches==

[[File:Histogram-rules.png|thumb|10000 samples from a normal distribution data binned using different rules. The Freedman-Diaconis rule results in 61 bins, the Scott rule 48 and Sturges' rule 15.]]

With the factor 2 replaced by approximately 2.59, the Freedman–Diaconis rule asymptotically matches  [[Scott's Rule|Scott's rule]] for data sampled
from a normal distribution.

Another approach is to use [[Sturges's rule]]: use a bin width so that there are about <math> 1+\log_2n </math> non-empty bins, however this approach is not recommended when the number of data points is large.<ref name="scott" />
For a discussion of the many alternative approaches to bin selection, see Birgé and Rozenholc.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Birgé | first1 = L. | last2 = Rozenholc | first2 = Y. | year = 2006 | title = How many bins should be put in a regular histogram | url = http://www.numdam.org/item?id=PS_2006__10__24_0 | journal = ESAIM: Probability and Statistics | volume = 10 | pages = 24–45 | doi=10.1051/ps:2006001|doi-access=free }}</ref>
